title: The Way, the Truth, and the Life; the Promise of the Advocate
summary: Jesus comforts his troubled disciples: he is going to prepare a place for them in his Father's house and will come back for them. He tells Thomas that he is the way and the truth and the life, and tells Philip that whoever has seen him has seen the Father. He promises another Advocate, the Spirit of truth, who will be with them and teach them, and he leaves them his peace before rising to go.
story: Jesus has just told the disciples that he is leaving, that one of them will betray him, and that Peter will deny him (13:21-38). Chapter 14 answers their fear. It opens and nearly closes with the same words, “Do not let your hearts be troubled” (14:1, 27). The whole chapter explains how his going away will be for their good: he goes to prepare a place, the Father will send the Spirit, Jesus and the Father will make their home with those who love him, and his peace will remain. Questions from Thomas, Philip, and Judas (not Iscariot) move the conversation along, each revealing how little the disciples yet understand, and each drawing out more of who Jesus is.
historical:
The setting is still the meal on the night before Jesus' death, in Jerusalem at Passover time. Jesus' words take the form of a farewell speech, a pattern well known in Israel's Scriptures and later Jewish writing. Jacob blesses his sons before his death (Genesis 49), Moses delivers the whole book of Deuteronomy as a farewell, Joshua and David give final charges (Joshua 23-24; 1 Kings 2), and Jewish works written in the centuries around Jesus' time, such as the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, imagine the final words of Jacob's sons. Such speeches typically announce the leader's departure, comfort the followers, give commands, warn of trouble ahead, and name a successor. John's farewell discourse has all these features, but with a difference: the one who departs promises to come back, and the successor is the Spirit of God himself.

The disciples were Jews of modest background who had left homes and work to follow Jesus, and within hours they would scatter. The world in this chapter (14:17, 19, 22, 27, 30) doesn't mean the created earth or any one people. In John it usually means human society organized in rejection of God, and its prince (14:30) is the devil. Jewish and Gentile rulers alike will act on its behalf in the coming chapters.
cultural:
“In My Father’s house are many rooms” (14:2) would bring two pictures to mind. One is the extended family household, where sons added rooms to their father's house when they married, so that the family lived together. The other is the temple, which Jesus had called “My Father’s house” in 2:16 and which had many chambers around its courts. The word translated rooms (monē) means a dwelling place, somewhere to stay, and John uses the same root when Jesus says he and the Father will make their home with the one who loves him (14:23). The promise is less about real estate than about belonging to the Father's household.

Peace (Hebrew shalom) was the ordinary Jewish greeting and farewell, and it meant more than calm: wholeness, well-being, right relationship with God and others. Jesus uses the usual farewell, and then says his peace is not the kind the world gives (14:27). To be left as orphans (14:18) was a picture of vulnerability; in the ancient world orphans had no one to protect or provide for them, and disciples of a teacher who died could be described in the same way.
literary: The chapter is dialogue that becomes monologue. Thomas (14:5), Philip (14:8), and Judas (14:22) each ask a question that shows a misunderstanding, and Jesus' answers carry the teaching forward. The sixth “I am” saying stands near the start: “I am the way and the truth and the life” (14:6). Themes circle and return, a style typical of John: going and coming, loving and keeping commandments, the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father, the promise of the Spirit (14:16-17, 26). Jesus' last words, “Get up! Let us go on from here” (14:31), are followed by three more chapters of teaching, which has led many scholars to think chapters 15 to 17 were added to an earlier form of the discourse, while others think Jesus and the disciples left the room and he continued speaking on the way, or that the words mark a turning to face what is coming rather than a change of place.

outline.t: Many rooms in the Father's house
Thomas: I am the way and the truth and the life
Philip: whoever has seen me has seen the Father
Another Advocate, the Spirit of truth
The Spirit will teach; my peace I give you

doctrines.note: Jesus promises “another Advocate to be with you forever” (14:16), the Spirit of truth who will dwell in the disciples, teach them all things, and remind them of what Jesus said (14:26). The Spirit is personal, sent by the Father in the Son's name, and continues Jesus' own presence with his people.

The chapter speaks of Father, Son, and Spirit as distinct and yet one in presence: the Father dwells in the Son, the Spirit is sent in the Son's name, and the Father and the Son come to make their home with believers. When Jesus says “the Father is greater than I” (14:28), the church, especially after the fourth-century controversy with Arius, understood this of the Son's relation as Son and his humble state in the incarnation, not of a lesser divine nature.
“Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father” (14:9). Jesus is the full and personal revelation of God. What God is like is not guessed at from a distance but seen in the face and deeds of Jesus.

Jesus promises to do whatever the disciples ask in his name (14:13-14). Asking in his name means asking as his representatives, in line with his character and purposes, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son.

words.note: Paraklētos, Advocate, Helper, Counselor, or Comforter; translations vary because the word covers several roles. Its root sense is one called alongside, and in Greek it often meant a legal advocate or supporter in court. In John it names the Holy Spirit (14:16, 26; 15:26; 16:7), and in 1 John 2:1 the same word names Jesus as our advocate with the Father. When Jesus says another Advocate, he implies that he has been the first.

Hodos, way, road, or path. Thomas asks how they can know the way, and Jesus answers that he himself is the way (14:6). In the Old Testament the way of the Lord describes both how God acts and how his people should live (Psalm 25:4-5; Isaiah 40:3). Early Christians were known as followers of the Way (Acts 9:2).

Monē, a dwelling place or room, from the verb menō, to remain or abide. It appears in 14:2 for the rooms in the Father's house and in 14:23 for the home the Father and the Son will make with the believer. The link suggests that the promise of a future place and the present gift of God's presence belong together.

Orphanos, orphan, one bereft of parents or protector. “I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you” (14:18). Jesus assures the disciples that his going will not leave them alone; he will come to them in the resurrection and through the Spirit.

christ: The chapter shows Jesus as the only way to the Father because he is the one who has come from the Father and shares his life. He is not one guide among many pointing toward God; he is the truth and the life himself, and in him God is seen. The Old Testament longed to see God: Moses asked to see his glory (Exodus 33:18), and Philip's request echoes that longing. Jesus answers that the longing is met in him. The chapter also shows his care for the disciples on the night of his own suffering. Facing betrayal and death, he spends his last hours comforting them.

hard.q: Isn't it narrow and arrogant for Jesus to say that no one comes to the Father except through him?
hard.a:
Many thoughtful people find 14:6 the most offensive verse in the Gospel, since it seems to dismiss the sincere faith of others. Several things can be said. The claim is made not by Jesus' later followers but by Jesus himself, on the night of his death, to frightened friends; it is offered as comfort that there is a way to God, not as a boast. The claim also follows from what John says Jesus is: if he is the Word who was with God and was God (1:1), then to come to the Father through him is to come to God through God. A merely human teacher saying this would be arrogant; the question is whether Jesus is who he claims to be.

Christians have held different views about what the verse implies for those who never hear of Jesus. Some hold that explicit faith in Christ is necessary for salvation; others that Christ saves some who respond to the light they have without knowing his name; a minority hope all will finally be saved through him. All of these are views about how Christ saves, not whether it is through him, and they differ on a question the church has not settled with one voice. What John insists on is that Jesus is not one option among many but the way God himself has opened.

questions: Jesus answers the disciples' fear with his own presence rather than a full explanation. When have you needed a person more than an answer?
Philip wanted to see the Father. What does it change about your picture of God to look at Jesus?
Jesus ties loving him to keeping his commands. How do love and obedience relate in your own life with God?
